title: The Fuel Logistics Tail
lede: Most of the effort behind powering a fixed installation is not generation but the long chain that moves fuel to it, and that chain is a vulnerability.
body: A generator at a fixed defense installation is only the last link in a long chain. Behind it sits production, refining, storage, transport hubs, road or rail movement, and last-mile delivery. This chain is the logistics tail. For diesel- and gas-fed sites the tail runs continuously: the generator is never independent of it because stored fuel is finite and must be replenished.

Each link adds delay, cost-in-lives exposure, and a failure mode. A generator that runs perfectly still goes dark if any upstream link is cut. This is why energy security is a supply-chain problem, not only a hardware problem.

The breeder (Hyperion) and burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) are design-and-simulation studies, not built machines. Their relevance to logistics is the fuel side: fusion fuels are extraordinarily energy-dense, so a comparable amount of stored energy occupies a tiny fraction of the mass and volume of diesel. In principle that shortens the tail. In practice the burner faces four honest physics gates that are not yet closed, so no site-power claim is being made today.
The tail is continuous for combustion generators; it never ends
Every upstream link is a single point of failure
Fusion fuel density could shorten the tail in principle
The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) remains gated at the design stage

A useful way to size the tail is by its cadence: how often each link must act to keep the generator fed. A high-consumption site drives a fast cadence through every upstream link, multiplying the number of movements, handoffs, and storage turnovers that can fail. Slowing that cadence, by cutting demand or raising per-delivery energy, reduces failure opportunities at every link simultaneously, not just at the last one.
See the companion pages on the convoy problem and the qualitative cost-in-lives of resupply for how the tail translates into operational risk.

title: The Fuel Convoy Problem
lede: Moving fuel to where it is consumed concentrates risk onto a predictable, repeated, exposed movement that an adversary can target.
body: A fuel convoy is a repeating pattern: known origins, known destinations, roads that cannot change much, and a schedule driven by consumption rate. Predictability is the core weakness. The more fuel a site burns, the more often the convoy must run, and the more exposure accumulates over time.

The relationship is direct: consumption rate sets resupply frequency, and resupply frequency sets exposure. Reducing on-site fuel demand, or extending the interval between deliveries, reduces the number of exposed movements. Fusion fuels matter here because of their energy density, which in principle lengthens the interval between resupplies dramatically.

Convoys can be hardened with armor, escorts, and route variation, but hardening does not remove the movement; it only makes each movement more expensive in effort and personnel. Removing or greatly reducing the movement is categorically stronger than protecting it. That is the logistics argument for on-site, long-fuel-interval generation.
Convoys are predictable in origin, route, and cadence
Higher consumption means more frequent, more exposed movements
Hardening protects the movement; demand reduction removes it
Energy-dense fuel lengthens the resupply interval

Route variation, timing changes, and decoys can reduce predictability, but they cannot make a repeating requirement disappear; the destination and the consumption rate remain fixed. That is why analysts treat convoy exposure as a function of demand rather than of tactics. The tactics manage residual risk after the demand is set; only lowering the demand changes the size of the problem the tactics must cover.
This page describes a logistics principle. The fusion machines that could act on it are still design-and-simulation studies subject to the honest gates documented elsewhere in this section.

title: Cost in Lives of Fuel Convoys
lede: The true cost of fuel logistics is measured in the people exposed to move it, not in any monetary figure, and that cost scales with consumption.
body: Cost measured in exposure, not currency

This page deliberately avoids any monetary framing. The relevant cost of moving fuel is the people placed at risk to move it: drivers, escorts, maintenance crews, and route-security personnel. Every delivery run is a exposure event. The cumulative human cost of fuel logistics is the sum of these exposures over the life of an operation.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 124" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="who is exposed" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><circle cx="18" cy="20" r="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="34" y="24" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Drivers operating on fixed, predictable routes</text><circle cx="18" cy="46" r="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="34" y="50" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Escort and route-security personnel</text><circle cx="18" cy="72" r="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="34" y="76" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Recovery and maintenance crews for disabled vehicles</text><circle cx="18" cy="98" r="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="34" y="102" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5">Personnel time diverted from primary missions</text></svg>

Because exposure scales with the number of deliveries, and deliveries scale with consumption, cutting on-site fuel demand is a direct reduction in the number of people who must be placed at risk. This is the humanitarian core of the logistics argument, independent of any economic accounting.
How generation choice changes the exposure

A site that generates its own power from an energy-dense fuel needs resupply rarely, or over intervals measured in long horizons rather than days. Fewer resupply events means fewer exposure events. The breeder and burner are design studies today, so this is stated as intent and principle, not as a delivered capability.
Cost here is human exposure, not money
Exposure scales linearly with delivery frequency
Delivery frequency scales with on-site consumption
Reducing demand reduces the people placed at risk

Exposure also compounds indirectly. Personnel and vehicles committed to fuel movement are unavailable for the primary mission, and the security effort that protects convoys draws down the same finite pool of people. So each delivery imposes both a direct exposure and an opportunity cost in diverted capacity. Reducing delivery frequency returns that capacity to the mission while lowering the number of people directly at risk.
The honest gates on the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) mean this benefit is not available today; it is the reason the physics work matters.

title: Logistics Tail and Operational Tempo
lede: The size of the logistics tail sets a ceiling on how fast and how far an operation can move, because power demand travels with the force.
body: Operational tempo, the rate at which activities can be sustained, is bounded by the slowest supply constraint. For power-hungry fixed sites, fuel is often that constraint. When power demand must be met by continuous resupply, tempo is limited by how fast and how safely fuel can arrive.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 112" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="tempo constraint" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="10" y="45" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Combustion site (fuel-limited)</text><rect x="210" y="33" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="33" width="358.7" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="45" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">resupply-bound</text><text x="10" y="79" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">On-site dense-fuel (design intent)</text><rect x="210" y="67" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="67" width="84.4" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="79" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">resupply-light</text></svg>

When power is generated on site from an energy-dense fuel with long resupply intervals, tempo decouples from the fuel-delivery schedule. Planners gain freedom because the power constraint is no longer a moving target that must be re-supplied on a short cycle.

The benefit is not only fewer convoys; it is planning simplicity. A predictable, long-horizon fuel need is easier to schedule, protect, and reason about than a continuous short-cycle demand. This reduces the cognitive and logistical load on planners.
Tempo is bounded by the slowest supply constraint
Fuel is often that constraint for power-heavy sites
Dense on-site fuel decouples tempo from resupply cadence

There is a second-order effect: when tempo is fuel-limited, planners must hold reserve fuel and reserve transport against surges, which enlarges the very inventory and movement they are trying to protect. Decoupling tempo from resupply lets planners hold a smaller, steadier fuel posture, because demand no longer spikes the delivery schedule. The planning benefit and the exposure benefit reinforce each other, since fewer surge deliveries mean both simpler schedules and fewer exposed movements at exactly the moments operations are most stressed.
As with all pages here, the fusion machines that would enable this are design-and-simulation studies subject to the documented honest gates.

title: Fuel Resupply as an Attack Surface
lede: Every link that must be replenished is a surface an adversary can attack; reducing replenishment shrinks that surface.
body: In security terms, an attack surface is the set of points where a system can be disrupted. A continuously replenished fuel chain has a large surface: production, storage, transport nodes, and the last mile are all attackable, and each must be defended every cycle. The surface exists precisely because replenishment is continuous.

Reducing the frequency of replenishment reduces how often each of these points is exposed. Eliminating short-cycle resupply, in the limit, collapses much of the surface to the site itself. Energy-dense on-site generation is attractive precisely because it minimizes the replenishment surface.

Shrinking the surface does not remove the need for site hardening, physical security, and cyber protection. It changes the shape of the problem from defending a long moving chain to defending a fixed point. Fixed points are generally easier to protect than distributed, mobile chains.
Continuous replenishment = large, recurring attack surface
Each transport node must be defended every cycle
Long resupply intervals shrink the exposed surface
Fixed sites are easier to defend than moving chains

Surface also has a temporal dimension: a link is only exposed while it is active. A chain that resupplies daily presents its full surface every day; one that resupplies over long horizons presents it rarely. Reducing cadence therefore shrinks the surface in time as well as in structure, which is why long-interval on-site generation is treated as a surface-reduction measure and not merely a convenience.
The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) that could enable minimal-resupply site power is a design-and-simulation study; its honest gates are documented separately.

title: Energy Density: Fusion vs Diesel
lede: Fusion fuels store orders of magnitude more energy per unit mass than combustion fuels, which is the physical basis for a shorter logistics tail.
body: The mass and volume of fuel a site must store and resupply is set by two things: how much energy it needs and how much energy each unit of fuel carries. Combustion fuels release chemical-bond energy, on the order of tens of megajoules per kilogram. Fusion of light nuclei releases nuclear-binding energy, roughly a million times greater per unit mass. This gap is the entire logistics argument.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 112" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="energy per unit mass (log-scale intent)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="10" y="45" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Diesel (chemical energy)</text><rect x="210" y="33" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="33" width="8.4" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="45" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">~46 MJ/kg class</text><text x="10" y="79" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">D-T / D-3He fusion (nuclear)</text><rect x="210" y="67" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="67" width="422.0" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="79" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">~10^6x greater per kg</text></svg>

The bar above is schematic; the real ratio is so large it cannot be drawn to linear scale. The practical consequence is that the fuel a combustion site must move over years could, in fusion terms, occupy a small container. This is why fusion is discussed in a logistics context at all.

Energy density alone does not deliver power. The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) must also confine and convert that energy, and it faces four honest gates: plug-coil overstress, an operating regime far beyond any existing device, a helium-3 fuel demand far beyond terrestrial supply, and an availability shortfall against hyperscale standards. Density is the promise; the gates are the reason it is not yet real.
Fusion releases nuclear-binding energy (~10^6x more per kg)
Density is the physical basis for a short logistics tail
Confinement, conversion, and supply gates remain open

The density gap also reshapes storage safety. A large diesel inventory is a concentrated chemical-fire hazard that must be separated, bunded, and defended; a fusion fuel inventory of equivalent energy is physically small. The hazard character changes entirely, from bulk combustible storage to a small quantity of light-isotope fuel. This is a distinct benefit from the resupply-interval benefit, both flowing from the same density fact.
Fusion fuel density is a physics fact; a fielded generator is not. The two must not be conflated.

title: Reducing the Logistics Tail
lede: The logistics tail shrinks along three levers: less demand, denser fuel, and longer resupply intervals; fusion acts mainly on the second and third.
body: The logistics burden of powering a site is the product of demand, resupply frequency, and per-delivery exposure. Reducing any factor reduces the burden. Efficiency measures cut demand; energy-dense fuel and larger on-site storage extend the interval between resupplies. Fusion's contribution is concentrated in fuel density and resupply interval.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="logistics reduction levers" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85.0" y="50" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Cut demand</text><text x="85.0" y="68" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">efficiency</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269.0" y="50" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Denser fuel</text><text x="269.0" y="68" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">fusion lever</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453.0" y="50" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Longer interval</text><text x="453.0" y="68" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">fusion lever</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637.0" y="50" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Shorter tail</text><text x="637.0" y="68" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">result</text></svg>

No single lever removes the tail. Efficiency has diminishing returns; storage has physical and safety limits for combustion fuels. Fusion fuel density changes the storage and interval math by orders of magnitude, which is why it is the lever with the most headroom, if the machine can be built.

In the near term, demand reduction and conventional resilience measures are the available levers because the fusion machines are design-and-simulation studies. The fusion lever is a longer-horizon addition, gated on the breeder timeline (construction Q2 2027, first tritium around 2030) and, for site power, on closing the burner gates.
Burden = demand x frequency x per-delivery exposure
Efficiency cuts demand but has diminishing returns
Fusion fuel density extends resupply intervals
The fusion lever is longer-horizon and gate-limited

The three levers also differ in who controls them. Demand reduction is an operator choice available now; storage expansion is limited by safety codes and site area for combustion fuels; fuel density is fixed by chemistry and physics and only changes by changing the fuel. This is why fusion is framed as a change in kind rather than in degree: it moves the density lever that conventional measures cannot touch.
This is a framework, not a claim of delivered capability.

title: Last-Mile Fuel Delivery Risk
lede: The final leg of fuel delivery concentrates risk because it is the least flexible, most observed, and hardest-to-reroute part of the chain.
body: Why the last mile is worst

Upstream links in a fuel chain can often be rerouted, buffered, or duplicated. The last mile, the final approach to a specific site, usually cannot. There are few roads, the destination is fixed, and the pattern is observable. This makes the last mile the highest-exposure segment per unit of fuel delivered.

Site placement is often constrained by mission, terrain, and access, which limits last-mile flexibility further. A site chosen for its mission value may sit at the end of a single vulnerable approach. Reducing its fuel dependence is one of the few ways to lower last-mile risk without moving the site.
Upstream links are reroutable; the last mile usually is not
Last-mile events are the highest-exposure per unit fuel
Mission-driven siting often locks in last-mile exposure

Because the last mile is fixed and observable, it is also the segment where timing patterns are hardest to disguise. Deliveries must arrive at a working site on a cadence set by consumption, so an observer can infer the schedule from the load itself. Removing routine deliveries denies that inference. Rare, irregular resupply is far harder to pattern than a steady operational cadence.
The generators that could minimize resupply are design-and-simulation studies subject to the honest gates.

title: Energy Resilience Overview
lede: Resilience is the ability of a site to keep its critical loads powered through disruption; it is a property of the whole supply chain, not one generator.
body: Energy resilience is the capacity to maintain power to critical functions during and after a disruption, whether the disruption hits the grid, the fuel chain, or the generation hardware. A site is resilient only if no single failure takes down its critical loads. Resilience is therefore a systems property, spanning generation, storage, fuel supply, and control.

Two dependencies dominate for most fixed installations: the utility grid and the fuel resupply chain. A grid-tied, fuel-fed site inherits the failure modes of both. Reducing dependence on either raises resilience. On-site generation from an energy-dense fuel addresses both at once, in principle.

Resilience is built in layers: prime power, backup generation, energy storage, load prioritization, and islanding capability. Each layer covers a different failure mode. No fusion machine replaces this layered design; the design intent for the burner is to serve as a resilient prime-power layer that is not itself dependent on continuous resupply.
Resilience = keeping critical loads up through disruption
It is a whole-chain property, not a single generator
Grid and fuel chain are the dominant dependencies
Layered design covers distinct failure modes

Resilience is measured, not asserted. Useful metrics include ride-through depth (how long critical loads survive a disruption), recovery time, and the number of independent failures a site can absorb before losing its mission. A site can score well on one and poorly on another, so resilience claims should always name the metric. The burner concept is evaluated the same way, and its availability figure is one such metric stated openly.

The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is a design-and-simulation study with four open honest gates, including an availability shortfall against hyperscale standards; it is not a fielded resilience solution today.

title: Grid-Independent Operations
lede: A site that can operate without the utility grid removes one of the two largest single points of failure in its power supply.
body: Grid-independent operation means a site can power its critical loads without drawing from the utility grid, either continuously or during grid outages. Grid dependence is a strategic vulnerability: grids are large, distributed, and exposed to weather, physical attack, and cyber disruption. A site that can run islanded is insulated from grid-wide failures.

Grid independence is not the same as fuel independence. A diesel-backed site is grid-independent only as long as its fuel lasts, so it trades a grid dependency for a fuel dependency. True independence requires both: no grid reliance and no short-cycle fuel reliance. Energy-dense on-site generation is the design path toward both.

There is a difference between a generator sized to carry the site as prime power and one sized only to bridge outages. Backup-only generation still leaves the site grid-dependent in normal operation. The design intent for the burner (Aegis) is prime power, though the honest gates mean this is not yet demonstrable.
Grid independence removes a major single point of failure
Diesel backup trades grid dependence for fuel dependence
Full independence needs no-grid and no-short-cycle-fuel
Prime power differs from bridging backup

Grid independence also changes the failure correlation. A grid-tied site fails whenever the regional grid fails, so many sites go down together in a wide-area event. Independent on-site generation de-correlates those failures: one site's outage no longer implies its neighbors'. For a distributed set of critical facilities, de-correlated failure is often more valuable than a marginal improvement in any single site's uptime.
These are design principles; the enabling machines remain simulation studies.

title: Microgrids and Islanding
lede: A microgrid can disconnect from the wider grid and run as a self-contained island, keeping critical loads powered when the grid fails.
body: A microgrid is a local network of generation, storage, and loads that can operate connected to the utility grid or disconnected from it. The act of disconnecting and running self-contained is called islanding. Islanding lets a site ride through grid disturbances without losing its critical loads, then resynchronize when the grid recovers.

The quality of an island depends on its prime power. A microgrid islanded onto diesel is limited by fuel; islanded onto intermittent renewables it needs large storage. An energy-dense, long-fuel-interval generator would make islanding sustainable over long horizons, which is the design role envisioned for the burner.

Islanding requires fast fault detection, uninterrupted transfer, frequency and voltage control while disconnected, and safe resynchronization. These are mature engineering problems for conventional sources. Integrating a fusion generator as a microgrid asset would add its own control and startup requirements, none of which are demonstrated at the design stage.
Microgrids can run grid-tied or islanded
Island quality depends on the prime power source
Dense-fuel generation would sustain long islands
Control, transfer, and resync are the engineering challenges

Microgrids also enable graceful partial operation. If prime power is reduced, the microgrid controller can shed lower-priority feeders and hold the critical ones, rather than collapsing the whole island. This pairs directly with load prioritization: the control system enforces the priority hierarchy during an island. A fusion prime source would have to expose the control interfaces such a scheme needs, which is a design-stage integration requirement.
The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is a design-and-simulation study; its four honest gates are documented separately.

title: Black Start and Cold Start
lede: Black start is the ability to bring power up from a fully de-energized state without help from the grid, a demanding requirement for any prime source.
body: A black start is the process of restoring a site or grid section from complete shutdown without drawing on an external supply. Most generators assume some external power to start; a black-start-capable source can bootstrap itself. For a sovereign site, black-start capability is what turns islanding from a bridge into a durable capability.

Fusion generators are demanding to start. A tandem-mirror burner requires energizing high-field magnets and establishing a plasma before it produces net output. Providing the bootstrap energy for that startup, and doing so from a de-energized state, is a real engineering requirement that any resilient deployment must solve.
Why this is honest to flag

Cold-start and black-start behavior for the burner is not demonstrated; it is a design consideration layered on top of the four physics gates. Stating it plainly is part of full-physics candor: a machine that cannot start without the grid is not grid-independent, regardless of its steady-state output.
Black start = restore from full shutdown, no external supply
It converts islanding into a durable capability
Fusion startup needs bootstrap energy for magnets and plasma
Cold-start behavior is undemonstrated at the design stage

Black-start capability is usually provided by a small, independent starting source, a battery bank or a compact generator, sized only to energize the prime source. For a fusion generator that starting source must supply magnet excitation and plasma initiation energy before any output exists. Designing and protecting that bootstrap chain is part of making the machine genuinely grid-independent rather than merely capable of steady-state operation once running.
This is a design-and-simulation consideration, not a delivered capability.

title: Long-Duration Power Without Resupply
lede: The strategic prize of energy-dense fuel is a site that runs for long horizons between resupplies, shrinking exposure and simplifying planning.
body: The interval between fuel deliveries is set by on-site consumption and stored energy. Combustion fuels store little energy per unit mass, so even a large tank buys a short interval at high load. Fusion fuels store roughly a million times more energy per unit mass, so a modest fuel inventory could, in principle, carry a site for a long horizon.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 112" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="resupply interval (schematic)" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="10" y="45" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Diesel inventory</text><rect x="210" y="33" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="33" width="50.6" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="45" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">days-class interval</text><text x="10" y="79" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Fusion fuel inventory (design intent)</text><rect x="210" y="67" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="67" width="400.9" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="79" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">long-horizon interval</text></svg>

A long resupply interval changes the security posture from a continuous logistics problem to an occasional one. Fewer deliveries mean fewer exposure events and simpler planning, the benefits discussed across this section. The magnitude of the interval is a direct consequence of fuel density.

Two caveats apply. First, the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is a design study whose gates are open. Second, the burner's helium-3 fuel demand is roughly 400x domestic supply per commercial unit, so the fuel itself is a supply problem even if the interval is long. This is why breeder-bred and lunar helium-3 pathways matter to the logistics story.
Fusion density enables long-horizon intervals in principle
Fewer deliveries means less exposure and simpler planning
He-3 demand ~400x domestic supply is a separate open gate

A long interval also improves the quality of the resupply that does occur. Rare deliveries can be scheduled deliberately, escorted heavily, and timed to favorable conditions, because they are not forced by an urgent daily demand. The logistics burden shifts from a continuous, reactive activity to an occasional, planned one. This qualitative change is as valuable as the raw reduction in delivery count.
The interval benefit is real physics; the fielded machine is not yet.

title: Redundancy and N+1
lede: Redundancy keeps critical loads powered when a unit fails; N+1 and higher configurations trade added units for tolerance of failures.
body: No single generator is perfectly reliable, so resilient sites deploy redundant units. N+1 means enough capacity to serve the load (N units) plus one spare, so any single unit can fail or be maintained without dropping the load. Higher schemes (N+2, 2N) tolerate more concurrent failures at the cost of more units and more fuel or fuel-equivalent.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 146" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="redundancy levels" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="10" y="45" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">N (no redundancy)</text><rect x="210" y="33" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="33" width="84.4" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="45" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">any failure = outage</text><text x="10" y="79" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">N+1</text><rect x="210" y="67" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="67" width="253.2" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="79" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">tolerates 1 failure</text><text x="10" y="113" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">2N</text><rect x="210" y="101" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="101" width="422.0" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="113" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">full duplicate</text></svg>

Redundancy interacts with availability. If each unit has modest availability, redundancy is how a site reaches high aggregate availability. This matters for the burner, whose single-unit availability at the design stage is estimated at 0.86-0.995, well short of the 0.99982 that hyperscale Tier III facilities expect. Redundancy is one lever to close part of that gap, but it does not erase it.

Each redundant unit adds capital, footprint, maintenance burden, and, for combustion sources, fuel. For a fusion generator it would also add fuel demand, which for the burner is already gated by helium-3 supply. Redundancy is a genuine resilience tool but must be reasoned about against these constraints.
N+1 tolerates one failure; 2N is a full duplicate
Redundancy raises aggregate availability from per-unit availability
Burner per-unit availability 0.86-0.995 vs Tier III 0.99982
More units mean more footprint, maintenance, and fuel demand

Redundancy is only effective if failures are independent. Two units that share a common fuel supply, control system, or cooling loop can fail together, defeating the redundancy on paper. Robust N+1 design therefore requires independent support systems, not just duplicate generators. For a fusion deployment this means independent fuel handling and controls per unit, a real design requirement layered on the underlying machine gates.
Availability figures here are design-and-simulation estimates, stated plainly.

title: Distributed vs Centralized Generation
lede: Distributing generation across many small sources trades efficiency for resilience; centralizing it does the reverse.
body: Power can be generated at a few large plants (centralized) or many small sources near the load (distributed). Centralized generation is efficient and easy to manage but creates concentrated targets and long transmission dependencies. Distributed generation is harder to coordinate but has no single point whose loss takes down everything.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 104" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="generation architectures" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="85.0" y="50" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Central plant</text><text x="85.0" y="68" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">one target</text><line x1="160" y1="54" x2="194" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="194" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="269.0" y="50" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Transmission</text><text x="269.0" y="68" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">long path</text><line x1="344" y1="54" x2="378" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="378" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="453.0" y="50" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Load</text><text x="453.0" y="68" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">dependent</text><line x1="528" y1="54" x2="562" y2="54" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="562" y="26" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="637.0" y="50" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">vs distributed</text><text x="637.0" y="68" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle">many sources</text></svg>

For defense resilience, distribution is generally preferred because it removes concentrated single points of failure. A fusion generator sized for a single fixed installation fits the distributed model: power made where it is used, with no long transmission line to defend.

Distributed architectures favor modular units that can be added incrementally. The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is conceived as unit-scale generation for a specific site rather than a central plant serving a region. This aligns with distributed-resilience thinking, though the machine remains a design-and-simulation study with open gates.
Distributed = resilient but harder to coordinate
Site-scale fusion fits the distributed model
No long transmission line to defend

Distribution also changes the consequence of a successful attack or fault. Against a central plant, one success is catastrophic; against a distributed set, one success is a degradation. This shifts an adversary's calculus, because disabling distributed generation requires many coordinated successes rather than one. The trade is coordination overhead: distributed systems need control and synchronization that a single plant does not, and that coordination itself must be made resilient so it does not reintroduce the single point of failure distribution was meant to remove.
Architecture choice is independent of whether the specific machine is ready; the burner is not yet.

title: Critical Load Prioritization
lede: When power is constrained, resilience depends on shedding non-essential loads to keep the mission-critical ones running.
body: During a disruption, available power may not cover the full site demand. Resilience then depends on load prioritization: classifying loads by criticality and shedding the least important first, so the mission-critical loads stay up as long as possible. This is a control-and-planning discipline that operates regardless of generation source.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 180" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="load priority tiers" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="10" y="45" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Life-safety and command</text><rect x="210" y="33" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="33" width="422.0" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="45" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">never shed</text><text x="10" y="79" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Mission-critical systems</text><rect x="210" y="67" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="67" width="337.6" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="79" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">protect</text><text x="10" y="113" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Support functions</text><rect x="210" y="101" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="101" width="168.8" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="113" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">shed under stress</text><text x="10" y="147" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Convenience loads</text><rect x="210" y="135" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="135" width="63.3" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="147" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">shed first</text></svg>

A well-defined load hierarchy lets a site survive a reduced-power state gracefully rather than failing all at once. It also sizes the true resilience requirement: the prime source only needs to carry the top tiers through a disruption, not the entire nominal load.

Sizing a fusion generator to a site's critical-load tier, rather than its peak nominal load, changes the requirement substantially. This matters for the burner because its output, availability, and fuel demand are all constraints; serving a well-defined critical tier is a more tractable target than serving everything.
Prioritization keeps critical loads up under constraint
A load hierarchy sizes the true resilience requirement
Prime source need only carry top tiers through disruption
Critical-tier sizing eases fusion generator requirements

Prioritization must be defined in advance and automated, because a disruption is the wrong moment to negotiate which loads matter. Modern controllers encode the hierarchy and shed feeders automatically as available power falls. This makes the resilience outcome deterministic rather than dependent on operator judgment under stress. It also clarifies the true prime-power requirement, which is the sum of the tiers that must never be shed.
Load prioritization is available today; the fusion prime source is a design-and-simulation study.

title: Blackout Resilience for Critical Facilities
lede: Critical facilities must ride through grid blackouts without losing their mission; the depth of that ride-through is set by their power architecture.
body: A grid blackout is the reference disruption for resilience planning. Critical facilities, command centers, hospitals, communications hubs, must keep operating through it. Ride-through depth, how long the facility can sustain critical loads without the grid, is the key metric, and it is limited by on-site generation and fuel.

Diesel-backed facilities ride through only as long as fuel lasts, and extended blackouts have historically outrun on-site fuel stocks, forcing emergency resupply into exactly the conditions that caused the blackout. An energy-dense on-site source would extend ride-through from hours or days toward long horizons.

For hyperscale and Tier III-class facilities the bar is extreme: availability around 0.99982, meaning only tens of minutes of downtime per year. The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) at the design stage is estimated at 0.86-0.995 availability, roughly 30-100x short. It could contribute to a layered resilience architecture but is not a sole Tier III source today.
Ride-through depth is the key blackout metric
Diesel ride-through is fuel-limited and has been outrun
Dense on-site fuel extends ride-through toward long horizons
Burner availability 0.86-0.995 vs Tier III 0.99982 = 30-100x short

Extended blackouts are the stress case because they outrun the assumptions behind most backup designs. Backup generation is often sized for short outages, so a multi-day event forces emergency refueling under exactly the degraded conditions that caused the blackout. Designing for the long tail of outage duration, rather than the median, is what separates genuine resilience from nominal compliance, and it is where a long-fuel-interval source would matter most.
Availability numbers are design-and-simulation estimates, stated without softening.

title: Disaster Continuity of Operations
lede: In a disaster the grid and fuel chain are often the first casualties; continuity depends on power that does not rely on either.
body: Natural disasters tend to take down the grid and the fuel-delivery chain at the same time, and often the roads that resupply would use. Continuity of operations in a disaster therefore depends on power sources that are already on site and do not need short-cycle resupply through a damaged transport network.

This is the same logistics logic that applies in a defense context, arriving from a different direction: the resupply loop that is a vulnerability in conflict is a broken link in a disaster. Energy-dense on-site generation addresses both by minimizing dependence on external delivery.

Because the failure mode is shared, a generator designed for defense resilience is also relevant to disaster response and civilian critical infrastructure. Kronos treats the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) as a dual-use resilience concept, with civilian and humanitarian applications alongside defense ones. All remain design-and-simulation studies.
Disasters often take grid, fuel chain, and roads together
Continuity needs on-site power that avoids resupply
This mirrors the conflict logistics logic
The concept is dual-use: defense, disaster, civilian

Disasters also degrade the information needed to respond, because monitoring and communications lose power alongside everything else. Keeping a small set of coordination and communications loads energized preserves situational awareness, which multiplies the value of every other response resource. This is why continuity planning prioritizes command, communications, and medical loads first: powering them is what makes the rest of the response coherent, and why an on-site source that survives the event without resupply is valued above any capability that depends on a road network the disaster has already broken.
No fielded capability is claimed; the honest gates apply.

title: Defense Continuity of Operations
lede: Defense continuity requires that command, control, and critical systems keep power through any disruption, including deliberate attacks on infrastructure.
body: Defense continuity of operations means critical military functions, command and control, communications, sensing, keep running through disruption, including deliberate attacks on power infrastructure. Unlike disaster planning, the threat model includes an adversary who chooses to strike the grid or fuel chain precisely because they are load-bearing.

Against a deliberate adversary, dependencies are targets. Grid dependence and short-cycle fuel dependence are both exploitable. Sovereign on-site generation removes those levers, provided the generator itself is hardened and its rare fuel resupply is protected.

Continuity is layered: hardened facilities, redundant generation, load prioritization, and secure fuel. A fusion generator is one candidate prime-power layer, chosen for its long resupply interval. It does not replace the other layers, and at the design stage it is subject to the burner honest gates, including an availability shortfall against the most demanding continuity standards.
Threat model includes deliberate attacks on power
Dependencies are targets for an adversary
Sovereign generation removes grid and fuel levers
It is one layer among several, and remains gated

An adversary studying a fixed installation will map its dependencies precisely because dependencies are cheaper to attack than hardened endpoints. Removing the grid and short-cycle-fuel dependencies denies the two most attractive of those targets. What remains, a hardened on-site source and rare protected resupply, is a smaller and better-defended set. The security value is in the dependencies removed, not only in the capability added, and an evaluation that counts only the generator's output while ignoring the dependencies it eliminates will understate what the concept is for.
This describes design intent for a simulation-stage machine.

title: Continuity of Government and Critical Infrastructure
lede: The most essential civilian functions depend on power; sovereign generation is one way to keep them running when the grid cannot.
body: Continuity of government and critical-infrastructure protection rest on a small set of functions that must never go dark: emergency coordination, communications, water and medical systems, and financial and data infrastructure. All of these are electrically dependent, and most rely on a grid that is itself a critical infrastructure with well-known vulnerabilities.

Protecting these functions means either hardening the grid, which is a vast distributed problem, or giving each critical node its own resilient power. Node-level sovereign generation is attractive because it localizes the resilience requirement to the facilities that matter most.

Kronos frames these applications as civilian and dual-use first. The same on-site generation concept serves government continuity, hospitals, and data infrastructure as it does defense installations. The enabling burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is a design-and-simulation study with four open physics gates and is not offered as a fielded solution.
Essential functions are all electrically dependent
Grid hardening is a vast distributed problem
Node-level sovereign power localizes the requirement
Framing is civilian and dual-use first

These functions are also interdependent: communications depend on power, emergency coordination depends on communications, and medical and water systems depend on both. A power loss therefore cascades through the whole set. Node-level resilient power interrupts the cascade at its root by keeping the electrical layer up, which is why it is treated as foundational rather than as one measure among equals. Protecting the electrical layer first is the highest-leverage action available, because every other essential function is downstream of it and fails in sequence once it is lost.
Design stage; honest gates apply throughout.

title: Humanitarian and Disaster-Response Power
lede: Relief operations need reliable power exactly where infrastructure has failed; the logistics of powering them mirror the defense case.
body: Power at the point of need

Humanitarian and disaster-response operations set up in places where the grid is down and the fuel chain is broken. They need power for medical care, water purification, communications, and coordination, and they need it immediately, often for weeks. The logistics of getting fuel to a relief site is the same problem, and carries the same exposure, as a defense convoy.

Responders currently rely on generators and repeated fuel deliveries into damaged, dangerous areas. An energy-dense generator with a long resupply interval would reduce the number of relief-fuel runs, freeing transport capacity for people and supplies.

This is a direct dual-use application of the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) resilience concept, oriented toward relief rather than defense. The machine is a design-and-simulation study, and its helium-3 fuel and availability gates apply regardless of the humanitarian framing.
Relief sites lose both grid and fuel chain
Long-interval generation frees transport for people
This is a civilian dual-use of the burner concept

Relief logistics are also constrained by finite transport capacity into a damaged area, where every load of fuel displaces a load of people, water, or medical supplies. Reducing relief-fuel runs is therefore not only a safety measure but a capacity measure: it frees the scarce transport that a response depends on. The generation and logistics benefits are the same ones argued in the defense case, applied to saving lives directly, which is why Kronos treats the resilience concept as civilian and dual-use first rather than as a narrowly military capability.
Design stage; no fielded capability is claimed.

title: Sovereign Domestic Energy
lede: Sovereign energy means the fuel, generation, and critical isotopes a nation depends on are produced and controlled domestically, not imported.
body: Energy sovereignty is the capacity to supply critical energy and energy-related materials from domestic sources under national control, without dependence on foreign supply that can be interrupted for political or strategic reasons. It spans two things in the Kronos context: on-site generation for resilient power, and domestic production of strategic isotopes.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 180" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="sovereign supply flow" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><line x1="200" y1="60" x2="238" y2="70" stroke="#7a4a4a" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4 3" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line x1="440" y1="65" x2="500" y2="80" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line x1="440" y1="120" x2="500" y2="95" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="30" y="20" width="180" height="44" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#7a4a4a" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="120" y="41" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Foreign supply</text><text x="120" y="57" fill="#7a4a4a" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">fragile / gated</text><rect x="210" y="20" width="180" height="44" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="300" y="41" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Breeder (Hyperion)</text><text x="300" y="57" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">D-T neutrons</text><rect x="210" y="90" width="180" height="44" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="300" y="111" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Lunar He-3</text><text x="300" y="127" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">~2038-40 gate</text><rect x="430" y="55" width="180" height="44" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="520" y="76" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">Domestic stock</text><text x="520" y="92" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">tritium / He-3</text></svg>

The breeder (Hyperion) and burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) straddle both. The breeder is an isotope platform producing tritium, helium-3, and 14 MeV neutrons domestically; the burner is a resilient on-site generator concept. Together they map onto the two halves of sovereignty: materials and power.
Why isotopes are a sovereignty issue

Several strategic isotopes have thin, foreign-dominated, or shortage-prone supply chains. Helium-3 in particular has demand that outstrips supply. Domestic breeding changes the dependency picture, though the breeder is a design-and-simulation study whose tritium breeding ratio is treated as a design lever (1.1 / 1.5 / 1.8) rather than a settled number.
It spans on-site power and strategic isotopes
Breeder = isotope platform; burner = resilient generator
Helium-3 supply is a specific sovereignty pressure point

Sovereignty is not autarky. The goal is not to produce every input domestically but to remove the specific dependencies that an adversary or a disruption could exploit for leverage. Some inputs are safe to source globally; a few, thin-supply strategic isotopes and continuous critical power, are not. Sovereign capability targets that short, high-leverage list, which is exactly where the breeder and burner concepts are aimed.
All capabilities described are at the design-and-simulation stage.

title: Strategic Isotope Supply
lede: The breeder produces isotopes with defense and national-security value; domestic production of these is a strategic capability in its own right.
body: Some isotopes are strategic because they are essential to defense, security, or high-technology functions and are hard to obtain. The breeder (Hyperion) is designed to produce three: a tritium-class output (~4 kg/yr class), helium-3 (~1.97 kg/yr), and a stream of 14 MeV neutrons usable for materials and electronics work. Each maps to a distinct national-security need.

The breeder is a design-and-simulation study; construction is planned to begin Q2 2027 with first tritium around 2030 at the first-of-a-kind unit. The tritium breeding ratio is a design lever spanning 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8, not a fixed achievement. Output figures are design points, and no hardware net-gain claim is made before the first-of-a-kind unit.
Breeder produces tritium-class, helium-3, and 14 MeV neutrons
Each maps to a distinct national-security need
Domestic production decouples from fragile supply
Design stage; TBR is a lever (1.1/1.5/1.8), first tritium ~2030

The platform framing matters because it decouples value from net electricity. The breeder does not need to be a power plant to be strategically useful; its neutrons and bred isotopes have value while the machine simply runs at its design fusion power. This is why the breeder is evaluated as a materials facility, and why its economics are out of scope here: the analysis is about capability and supply, not generation.
This is the platform framing; economics are out of scope by policy.

title: Sovereign Tritium Supply
lede: Tritium is scarce, decays continuously, and has essential uses; domestic breeding is a route to a sovereign, replenishable supply.
body: Tritium is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen with a half-life of about 12.3 years, so any stockpile shrinks continuously and must be replenished. It has no large natural source and is expensive to produce, which makes existing supply thin and strategically sensitive. A domestic, renewable production route is therefore a sovereignty capability.

The breeder (Hyperion) breeds tritium by capturing fusion neutrons in a lithium blanket. Its design output is in the ~4 kg/yr class, with the tritium breeding ratio treated as a design lever across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8. A ratio above 1 means the machine can, in principle, breed more than it consumes, enabling a net supply, though this is a design target under study, not a demonstrated result.
Why the ratio is a lever, not a promise

Breeding ratio depends on blanket design, neutron economy, and losses that are still being characterized in simulation. Kronos treats it as a range precisely to avoid overclaiming. The honest reconciliation between local and net breeding is an open item flagged in the technical program.
Tritium half-life ~12.3 yr: stock decays and needs replenishment
No large natural source; existing supply is thin
Breeder output ~4 kg/yr class; TBR lever 1.1/1.5/1.8
Ratio is a design target under study, not demonstrated

Tritium also carries strict handling and accounting requirements because it is a mobile radioactive gas. A sovereign supply therefore implies sovereign stewardship: extraction, storage in getter beds, inventory accounting, and containment, all addressed in the safety and isotopes sections. Producing the material domestically only delivers sovereignty if the handling infrastructure is domestic and robust as well, which is part of the breeder program's scope.
Design-and-simulation stage; first tritium at the first-of-a-kind unit is targeted around 2030.

title: Helium-3 Strategic Supply
lede: Helium-3 is scarce and in chronic shortage; the breeder produces it, and the burner consumes it, which frames the whole sovereignty story.
body: Helium-3 is a light, stable isotope used in neutron detection, cryogenics, quantum systems, and as a candidate fusion fuel. It is extremely rare on Earth, and demand has outstripped supply for years. This scarcity is the pivot of the Kronos energy-security story because the same isotope is both a product of the breeder and the fuel of the burner.

The breeder (Hyperion) produces helium-3 at a design point of about 1.97 kg/yr, partly through tritium decay (tritium decays to helium-3). This is a domestic production route for a material with no reliable domestic source. But the burner's helium-3 fuel demand is roughly 400x domestic supply per commercial unit, so breeding alone does not close the fuel gap.
Why lunar helium-3 enters the picture

Because terrestrial helium-3, including breeder-bred helium-3, cannot meet burner-scale fuel demand, the long-horizon supply story includes lunar helium-3, gated to roughly 2038-40. This is stated plainly as a dependency, not a solved problem: the burner's fuel supply does not exist at terrestrial scale today.
He-3 is rare on Earth and in chronic shortage
Breeder produces ~1.97 kg/yr, partly via tritium decay
Burner He-3 fuel demand ~400x domestic supply per unit
Lunar He-3 (~2038-40) is a stated dependency, not solved

The dual role of helium-3, product of one machine and fuel of the other, is the single most important structural fact in this section. It means the breeder's isotope value and the burner's fuel gap are not separate stories but two ends of the same material chain. Reasoning about one without the other, at its correct scale, is the most common way the supply picture gets distorted.

title: 14 MeV Neutron Supply for Defense
lede: The breeder's stream of 14 MeV fusion neutrons is a domestic capability for materials qualification and detection-relevant work.
body: Every D-T fusion reaction releases a 14 MeV neutron. At the breeder's design point of 88.7 MW fusion power, the machine is a strong, steady source of fast neutrons. Such neutrons are useful for qualifying materials and electronics against radiation and for neutron-based inspection, capabilities relevant to national security and dependent today on scarce facilities.

A domestic fusion-spectrum neutron source reduces dependence on limited or foreign irradiation facilities for defense-relevant testing. This is a supply-security benefit distinct from power: the neutrons are a service, not electricity, and are available while the machine runs regardless of net-energy questions.

Detailed neutron applications, radiation-effects testing, materials qualification, and detection, are covered in the national-security and isotopes sections of this site. Here the point is narrow: a domestic 14 MeV source is a sovereignty asset. The breeder remains a design-and-simulation study, with the neutron output following from its design fusion power.
D-T fusion yields 14 MeV neutrons; 88.7 MW design power
Fast neutrons qualify materials and electronics
A domestic source reduces reliance on scarce facilities
Neutrons are a service, independent of net-energy questions

The steadiness of the source matters as much as its intensity. A neutron facility that runs predictably supports scheduled qualification campaigns, which is what materials and electronics programs need. Existing high-energy neutron sources are few and heavily subscribed, so a domestic, steady 14 MeV source relieves a genuine capacity constraint. That capacity value is independent of any net-energy question about the machine.
Design stage; the output is a design point, not a measured result.

title: Isotope Supply Independence from Imports
lede: Several strategic isotopes depend on foreign or fragile supply; domestic breeding reduces that dependence and its associated leverage.
body: When a critical isotope must be imported or comes from a single fragile source, the supplier holds strategic leverage: supply can be constrained for political reasons or lost to disruption. Helium-3 and tritium are both examples of materials where supply is thin and control is concentrated. Import dependence is a national-security vulnerability, not merely a procurement inconvenience.

Domestic breeding in the breeder (Hyperion) changes the dependency picture by creating a production route under national control. This does not automatically make supply abundant, especially for helium-3 at burner scale, but it removes the single-supplier and foreign-control failure modes for the quantities the breeder can produce.

Independence is partial and staged. The breeder is a design-and-simulation study; its output figures are design points; and its tritium breeding ratio is a lever (1.1 / 1.5 / 1.8). For helium-3 the domestic route does not meet burner fuel demand, which is why the lunar pathway is part of the long-horizon story. Independence should be described as reduced dependence, not eliminated dependence.
Import or single-source supply is strategic leverage
He-3 and tritium are thin, concentrated supply chains
Domestic breeding removes foreign-control failure modes
Independence is partial, staged, and design-stage

Dependence is also a peacetime risk, not only a wartime one. Supply can tighten because of a single facility's outage, a policy change abroad, or a demand spike in an unrelated sector, all without any deliberate action against the buyer. Domestic breeding hedges this ordinary volatility as well as adversarial interruption, which broadens the case for it beyond the conflict scenario.
No overclaim: this is reduced dependence at the design stage.

title: Lunar Helium-3 Supply Chain
lede: Because terrestrial helium-3 cannot meet burner-scale fuel demand, the long-horizon supply story depends on lunar helium-3, gated to roughly 2038-40.
body: A supply that does not yet exist at scale

The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is fueled by deuterium and helium-3. Its helium-3 fuel demand is roughly 400x domestic supply per commercial unit, a gap that breeder breeding alone cannot close. The candidate source at the required scale is helium-3 embedded in lunar regolith by the solar wind over geologic time, extracted and returned to Earth.

This is a long, unproven, and expensive-in-effort supply chain that does not exist today. Kronos states the gate plainly: burner-scale operation is dependent on a lunar helium-3 supply chain reaching maturity around 2038-40. Nothing about the burner's site-power role is available before that dependency is met.
Why it is in an energy-security section

The lunar dependency is the deepest logistics fact about the burner. The machine that would cut the terrestrial fuel-logistics tail depends, at scale, on a cislunar logistics chain. This is honest full-physics framing: the fuel-supply gate is as real as the plasma-physics gates and is the reason breeder-bred and lunar helium-3 both matter.
Burner He-3 demand ~400x domestic supply per unit
Breeder breeding cannot close the fuel gap alone
Lunar regolith is the candidate scale source, ~2038-40
Burner-scale operation is gated on this chain maturing

It is worth stating the trade in one sentence: the burner would replace a terrestrial fuel-logistics tail with a cislunar one. Whether that is worthwhile depends entirely on the extraction and return chain maturing, which is a program well outside Kronos's own machines. Kronos's honest position is to name the dependency and its rough timing, not to assert that the lunar chain will exist on schedule.
Stated as a dependency, not a solved capability; the burner is a design-and-simulation study.

title: Breeder-Bred Helium-3 Pathway
lede: The breeder produces helium-3 directly and through tritium decay, a domestic pathway that matters even though it cannot meet burner-scale demand.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) yields helium-3 by two routes. Some is produced in the plasma and blanket environment; more accumulates because tritium decays to helium-3 with a ~12.3-year half-life. Tritium bred and stored in the ~4 kg/yr class thus becomes a slow, steady helium-3 source over time. The design point for helium-3 output is about 1.97 kg/yr.

This pathway is strategically valuable for the many uses of helium-3 that need kilogram-scale quantities: neutron detection, cryogenics, and quantum systems. For those markets a domestic breeder-bred supply is meaningful and reduces reliance on the chronic global shortage.
It does not fuel the burner

The same pathway does not solve burner fuel supply, whose demand is roughly 400x domestic supply per commercial unit. Breeder-bred helium-3 and lunar helium-3 serve different scales: the former supplies detection and technology markets; the latter is the only candidate for burner-fleet fuel. Conflating them would overstate the near-term fuel picture.
He-3 comes directly and via tritium decay (~12.3 yr)
Design output ~1.97 kg/yr, tritium ~4 kg/yr class
Meaningful for detection, cryogenics, quantum markets
Does not meet burner fuel demand (~400x supply)

The decay route has a useful property: tritium held in a managed stockpile becomes a helium-3 source over time whether or not it is used as fuel, because decay proceeds regardless. This makes a tritium reserve a slow helium-3 generator, coupling the two isotope inventories. Accounting for both together, with their different half-lives and uses, is the substance of the flagged supply-balance reconciliation.
Design-and-simulation stage; a helium-3 supply-balance reconciliation is a flagged open item.

title: Strategic Isotope Reserve
lede: A domestic breeder makes possible a strategic reserve of scarce isotopes, buffering national capability against supply shocks.
body: A strategic reserve is a stockpile held against future disruption, the way nations hold reserves of critical commodities. For decaying isotopes like tritium and helium-3, a reserve is dynamic: tritium decays, and helium-3 accumulates from that decay, so the reserve must be actively managed. Domestic breeding is what makes maintaining such a reserve feasible without foreign dependence.

A managed reserve buffers national capability against supply shocks: a disrupted foreign source, a facility outage, or a demand spike. The buffer is only as strong as the production that replenishes it, which is why sovereign breeding and a reserve are complementary rather than alternatives.

A reserve does not create supply; it smooths it. For helium-3 at burner scale the underlying supply gap (~400x) is too large for any terrestrial reserve to bridge, so the reserve concept applies to detection, cryogenic, and technology-scale uses, not to burner fuel. The breeder that would stock the reserve is a design-and-simulation study.
A reserve buffers against supply shocks
Decaying isotopes need active reserve management
Reserve strength depends on replenishing production
It smooths supply but cannot bridge the He-3 fuel gap

A reserve also needs a policy for draw-down and replenishment, not just storage. For decaying isotopes the replenishment rate must at least offset decay plus withdrawals, or the reserve erodes silently. This turns a reserve into an active flow problem tied to breeder output, rather than a static stockpile. Designing that flow, and its accounting, is a prerequisite before any reserve claim would be meaningful.
Concept stage; no reserve exists, and the breeder is not built.

title: Isotope Supply-Chain Resilience
lede: Resilient isotope supply means multiple production routes, managed inventory, and no single point whose loss ends the supply.
body: The same resilience logic that applies to power applies to strategic materials. An isotope supply is resilient when it has redundant production, buffered inventory, and no single facility or supplier whose loss ends the supply. Thin, single-source isotope chains are the opposite: fragile by construction.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 146" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="isotope supply resilience" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="10" y="45" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Single foreign source</text><rect x="210" y="33" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="33" width="63.3" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="45" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">fragile</text><text x="10" y="79" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Single domestic source</text><rect x="210" y="67" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="67" width="211.0" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="79" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">better, still single</text><text x="10" y="113" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600">Fleet + reserve (design intent)</text><rect x="210" y="101" width="422" height="16" rx="3" fill="#1a212b" stroke="#3a4453" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="210" y="101" width="422.0" height="16" rx="3" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="638" y="113" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" font-weight="600">redundant + buffered</text></svg>

A breeder fleet, several units rather than one, would provide production redundancy, and a managed reserve would buffer demand shocks. This is the same N+1 thinking used for power, applied to material output. Fleet-scale production is part of the long-horizon strategy, not a current capability.

Today there is no breeder and no fleet; the first-of-a-kind unit targets first tritium around 2030, with subsequent units following. Resilience through redundancy is therefore a staged outcome, and helium-3 at burner scale remains gated regardless. The near-term resilience gain is for detection- and technology-scale isotope supply.
Resilient supply needs redundancy, buffer, no single point
Thin single-source chains are fragile by construction
A breeder fleet plus reserve gives redundancy and buffer
Fleet resilience is staged; He-3 at burner scale stays gated

Resilience for materials, as for power, is ultimately about de-correlated failure. Several independent breeder units with independent handling infrastructure fail independently, so a single outage degrades rather than ends supply. A single facility, however sovereign, does not offer this property. Fleet-scale redundancy is therefore the structural answer, and it arrives only as units are built out over the breeder program's staged timeline, which begins with a single first-of-a-kind unit and gains redundancy unit by unit rather than all at once.
Design-and-simulation stage; a fleet does not yet exist.

title: Aegis Fixed-Installation Power
lede: Aegis is the fixed-installation housing of the burner: a sovereign, on-site power concept for defense sites, not a naval or mobile system.
body: Aegis is one of two housings for the same underlying burner, a deuterium-helium-3 tandem-mirror generator. Aegis is intended for fixed defense installations: sited, stationary facilities. It is explicitly not a naval or mobile system. The value proposition is sovereign on-site power that minimizes dependence on the grid and on short-cycle fuel resupply.

Aegis being fixed rather than mobile is a deliberate scoping choice, not a limitation to apologize for. Fixed siting is what makes the machine's magnet systems, support infrastructure, and rare protected resupply tractable, and fixed installations are precisely the high-value sites where sovereign power matters most. The concept is honest about what it is: sited prime power for stationary facilities, gated by the burner physics.
No power-delivery claim is made today.

title: Burner as Resilient Power Source
lede: The burner is conceived as a resilient prime-power source: on-site, energy-dense-fueled, and independent of the grid, subject to open physics gates.
body: The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is a deuterium-helium-3 tandem-mirror generator with direct energy conversion. As a resilience concept it targets three properties at once: on-site generation (no long transmission line), energy-dense fuel (long resupply interval), and grid independence (no reliance on the utility). Together these address the dominant single points of failure in site power.

The tandem-mirror configuration uses a 26.49 T plug field and 17 T throat field to confine the plasma, with a neutron fraction of 5.44% because deuterium-helium-3 is a low-neutron fuel. Direct energy conversion turns charged-particle energy into electricity without a full thermal cycle, a feature attractive for compact, resilient generation.
Why the concept is not yet a capability

Four honest gates separate the concept from a fielded machine: plug-coil overstress (3-3.9x), an operating regime 166-830x beyond any device, helium-3 fuel demand ~400x domestic supply, and availability 0.86-0.995 versus Tier III 0.99982. These are physics findings from design and simulation, stated plainly because they define what must be solved.
Targets on-site, dense-fuel, grid-independent power at once
Tandem mirror: 26.49 T plug, 17 T throat, 5.44% neutron fraction
Direct energy conversion avoids a full thermal cycle
Four honest gates separate concept from capability

It is worth separating the three resilience properties, because they can be delivered partially. On-site siting and grid independence are architectural choices that many sources can offer; the long resupply interval is what fusion fuel density adds uniquely. A candid assessment credits fusion specifically for the interval and the small fuel footprint, while acknowledging that the architectural properties are shared with other on-site sources.
Design-and-simulation stage; no net-power hardware claim is made.

title: Burner Honest Gates for Defense
lede: Four physics gates separate the burner resilience concept from a fielded generator; each is stated as a design-and-simulation finding, not softened.
body: Full-physics candor requires naming the gates that stand between the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) concept and a real defense generator. These are physics facts from design and simulation, not economics. Any defense evaluation should treat them as the entry conditions for the technology to become relevant.

<svg viewBox="0 0 722 96" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Plug coil stress" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:722px;display:block;margin:18px 0;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="4.5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4.5 L0,9 z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="10" y="24" width="702" height="48" rx="6" fill="#232C39" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="26" y="46" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="14" font-weight="700">Plug coil stress</text><text x="26" y="63" fill="#F4EFE4" font-size="11">Overstressed at the design bore -> infeasible as specified.</text><text x="702" y="55" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="22" font-weight="800" text-anchor="end">3-3.9x</text></svg>
